name: Albiglutide
lead: Albiglutide (brand names Tanzeum in the United States and Eperzan in Europe) is a once-weekly injectable glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist that was approved to improve blood-sugar control in adults with type 2 diabetes. It was developed by Human Genome Sciences and marketed by GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) [11][1].

It is a fusion protein made of two copies of a modified human GLP-1 sequence attached to human albumin, a design that slows its breakdown and lets it be dosed weekly [11][1]. It was approved in Europe in March 2014 and in the US in April 2014, and GSK announced a worldwide withdrawal in 2017 for economic reasons [11].

Albiglutide was never approved for weight loss. It is covered here because it belongs to the GLP-1 class of drugs behind much of today's fat-loss discussion: GLP-1 drugs slow gastric emptying and reduce appetite, which lowers calorie intake, and sustained loss of body fat is what changes how the face and body look [4][15]. Albiglutide's own weight effect was modest, and a 2015 analysis cited on Wikipedia found it less effective than other GLP-1 agonists on both blood-sugar and weight measures [11]. It is no longer marketed anywhere.

paras: The approved use was as an add-on to diet and exercise for adults with type 2 diabetes [1][11]. It was not approved for obesity or cosmetic weight management, and no trial in the registry set out to test it as a weight-loss drug.

Like other GLP-1 receptor agonists, albiglutide mimics the gut hormone GLP-1, which raises insulin secretion when glucose is high, lowers glucagon, slows gastric emptying and may reduce appetite [4][3]. Native GLP-1 is degraded within a few minutes in the circulation, so analogues have been engineered for longer action [4].

Albiglutide is a recombinant protein of about 645 amino acids produced in yeast, in which a single amino acid change protects the GLP-1 portion from the enzyme DPP-4, and the albumin portion extends its life in the body [11]. Peak levels occur 3 to 5 days after an injection and the elimination half-life is about 5 days [11].

In the HARMONY phase 3 programme, albiglutide lowered HbA1c versus placebo and added to other diabetes drugs [1][13]. Grokipedia, citing the product label, reports HbA1c reductions of about 0.7 to 0.9 percentage points versus a small rise on placebo over 52 weeks as monotherapy, and up to 0.9 points when added to metformin or sulfonylureas [1]. HARMONY 1 tested it added to pioglitazone with or without metformin for 52 weeks, and another trial compared it with prandial insulin added to basal insulin [13][20].

In HARMONY 7, a head-to-head open-label trial against daily liraglutide, albiglutide met non-inferiority criteria on the pre-specified margin but is reported to have produced smaller reductions in HbA1c and body weight [9][11][21]. Systematic reviews and mixed-treatment comparisons place it at the lower end of the class for HbA1c and weight reduction [5][10][11][22].

Weight loss with GLP-1 agonists as a class is linked to delayed gastric emptying and appetite effects; reviews of gastric physiology describe how GLP-1 and its analogs slow emptying in people with diabetes and obesity [15]. Compared with newer agents such as semaglutide and tirzepatide, albiglutide's published weight effect is smaller [10][11].

Reported common effects in trials include diarrhoea, nausea, injection-site reactions and, with other glucose-lowering drugs, hypoglycaemia [11]. Gastrointestinal events are the most frequently reported class-wide adverse events in GLP-1 trials [7]. Acute pancreatitis (about 0.3% in trials) and hypersensitivity were reported as uncommon [11].

The US label carried a boxed warning about thyroid C-cell tumours, based on rodent findings seen with the class, and listed medullary thyroid carcinoma and multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 as contraindications [11][1].

An integrated analysis of seven phase 3 type 2 diabetes studies of up to three years evaluated albiglutide's safety against placebo and active comparators [14]. A published editorial described a case of albiglutide-associated pancreatitis [17]. Grokipedia lists a pregnancy category C classification, with no adequate human studies [1].

Human Genome Sciences invented the molecule and developed it with GSK, which later acquired the company. GSK filed for US approval in January 2013 and for European approval in March 2013 [11]. The European Commission approved it in March 2014 and the US FDA in April 2014 [11].
In 2017 GSK announced it would withdraw the drug worldwide by July 2018, citing economic reasons [11][1].

Wikipedia reports a 2015 analysis finding albiglutide caused fewer side effects overall than some other agents but more injection-site reactions than liraglutide [11]. The 2017 withdrawal announcement was made in August; remaining supply was effectively depleted by 2018 [11]. Grokipedia attributes the discontinuation to limited prescribing and commercial viability in a market where newer agents had broader indications [1].

Albiglutide was tested in a large phase 2 and 3 programme in type 2 diabetes, including trials in renal impairment (507 participants) [20][13], Japanese patients and a head-to-head trial against liraglutide with 841 participants [21]. A trial of 309 participants was among the first phase 3 studies, started in 2009 [13].

The Harmony Outcomes trial randomised patients aged 40 and older with type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, in 610 sites in 28 countries, to weekly albiglutide or placebo added to standard care, with a primary outcome of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or stroke [12]. The registered trial enrolled 9,463 participants [19]. Grokipedia reports a 22% reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events [1]. A post hoc analysis examined outcomes in older adults [18], and meta-analyses of GLP-1 agonist outcome trials have included albiglutide [2][23][24].

A 52-week phase 2 trial compared albiglutide with placebo in adults with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes [16]. A paediatric trial and an insulin add-on trial were registered but withdrawn before enrolment [13]. No trial studied it as an appearance or body-composition treatment in people without diabetes.

card.summary: A withdrawn once-weekly GLP-1 diabetes drug; it was never a weight-loss product and produced modest weight effects in trials.
card.note: No longer marketed anywhere; approved only for type 2 diabetes.

quick.overview:
Albiglutide was a weekly injection for type 2 diabetes in the same drug class as semaglutide and liraglutide. It was approved in 2014 and pulled from the market by GSK in 2017-2018 for commercial reasons.

It was never licensed for weight loss, and published comparisons rate its weight and blood-sugar effects as smaller than those of other drugs in its class.
quick.mechanism: It is a modified GLP-1 fused to albumin, which resists breakdown and lasts about five days in the body. It activates GLP-1 receptors, which raises insulin release after meals, lowers glucagon and slows stomach emptying.
quick.risks: Reported effects include nausea, diarrhoea and injection-site reactions, with pancreatitis uncommon. The label carried a boxed warning about thyroid C-cell tumours seen in rodent studies of the class. It is no longer sold.

Modest weight effect seen in diabetes trials
Not marketed for appearance; class-level interest in fat loss
angle.text: Albiglutide belongs to the GLP-1 drug family that people associate with appetite reduction and fat loss. It was a diabetes drug with a smaller weight effect than other class members, and it is no longer available.
